She went off Tobin’s chest in one bound and straight through the ring of Knights, between their grey legs, and down the slope of the Hill faster than Wren had ever seen her go, with her ears flat and her tail straight out behind her. And the spark at the end of her tail, which had been hardly anything for weeks, blazed. It went up like a torch. It streamed out behind her, so that she went down Cinder Hill like a little comet, a long gold streak across the grey ash; and Wren could hear her yelping as she went — not a fighting sound, but a high, glad, silly, puppyish sound, the sound a dog makes when somebody it loves comes home. She reached him at the foot of the Hill and threw herself at him. He bent and caught her up in both arms, the whole wriggling, yelping, blazing armful of her, and she licked his face and climbed onto his shoulder and nearly fell off the other side; and across the whole width of the Queen’s silent camp, Wren heard him laugh. It was a short laugh, not loud: the laugh of somebody who has been licked on the ear by a fox and does not mind. But every Hollow Knight on the Hill turned its head towards it at once, the way grass turns in a wind. He put Cinder down. And then he began to walk up the Hill. I have to tell you what he looked like, and I find that I cannot do it very well. This is not because he was too splendid to describe. It is because he was not splendid at all. He was a man, not especially tall and not especially broad. He wore a plain brown coat that had been travelled in a good deal, and mended boots, and there was dust on him to the knees. His face was brown and weathered, with a short beard going grey and lines at the corners of his eyes that came from laughing. He carried nothing. No lamp, no staff, no sword. His hands were empty at his sides. That was all. If you had passed him on the road you might not have looked at him twice — unless he had looked at you first. Then, I think, you would have remembered it all your life. But nobody was looking at him, just at first. They were looking at the ground. Because where he walked, the colour came back. It came up out of the ash behind his heels, the way water comes up into a footprint on a beach. Where he lifted his foot the ground was not grey. It was dark and rich and brown, the brown of new earth turned with a spade — and as Wren watched, in the very first footprint, a little thread of green came up and unrolled itself and stood there, trembling, in the cold dawn air. Then the next footprint, and the next. Behind him came a path of colour, brown and green and the warm red of the rock beneath, widening as it came, the way light widens across a floor when somebody opens a shutter. And the ground was warm. Wren felt it come up the slope towards her, under her knees, like a hearthstone. They say the ground there is still warm. She had heard that once, in a tower, by the light of a little lamp behind a sheet. He came to the edge of the Queen’s camp, and he did not stop. The Hollow Knights fell back. They did not shriek, the way the Hollows shrieked in Soot Lane. They simply went back from him as he came on, the way shadows go back from somebody walking into a room with a candle. He did not look at them. He did not lift a hand. Wherever he walked there was no room for them, and so they were not there. The ring of grey armour round Wren opened like a door. Some of the Knights sat down suddenly in the ash, like men who have been walking in their sleep and woken in a strange place. On the tent-poles the ash-crows went up all together in a grey clatter of wings, and flew away west, crying, and did not come back. The braziers that burned with no heat went out, one after another, as he passed them: not blown out, but simply finished, as though somebody had told them they could stop. And the lamp in Wren’s hands blazed. She had seen it blaze at the top of the Beacon, and at the foot of the Black Stair. She had never seen it do this. The flame went up inside its cracked chimney, gold and white and gold again, so bright that it filled the whole Hill; and it was not leaning any more, it was reaching. It reached towards the man coming up through the camp the way a flower in a window turns towards the sun, with its whole self, as though it had been growing that way all its life and had only just found out why. And the colour flooded. It ran out across the Hill from the lamp and from the man together, and met in the middle. The tents went the creamy, stained colour of old canvas. The ash went brown and black and rust-red. The stones of the workshop above them, grey for three hundred years, were suddenly a warm grey-gold, like a cat’s back in sunshine. The ribbon on Wren’s wrist went red — red as a coal, red as a berry, redder than she had ever seen it — and Tobin’s scarf round her own neck, which had never in all the grey been any colour she could have named, turned out to be striped. Green and blue. Green and blue, all the way down. She had been wearing it for weeks and never known. The Queen stood up. She was tall and slender and silver from head to foot, and she looked at the man coming up the Hill. Beside her, on its stand, the dark mirror cracked. Nobody touched it. It cracked of its own accord, with a small sharp sound like ice on a pond, one long crack from the top of the oval to the bottom; and whatever had been moving in it stopped moving, and it was only a piece of black glass with a crack in it. The Queen did not look at it. She was looking at him. She looked at him once. Only once. Wren saw her face as she did it, and I am not going to tell you what was in it, because Wren never would, not even to Mira, not even years afterwards. I will only say this. In all the time Wren had known that voice — in the dark at Emberwick, in the bottom of the boat at Vaelport, in the grey tent — it had never once been raised. It had never needed to be. The Queen screamed. It was a long, thin, terrible sound, like wind in a broken flue, and it was not a word. While it was still going on she turned in a whirl of silver and fled — away from the morning, out across the Burned Country towards the west, where the last of the night still lay low along the edge of the sky. She seemed to pour rather than run. The night took her in, and the scream went on a long time after Wren could no longer see her, smaller and smaller, until at last it stopped. The Hill was very quiet. Only one man in the camp had not fallen back. Captain Varrick stood alone in the trodden ash in front of the empty tent, in his grey armour and grey cloak, with his sword drawn. He did not lift it as the man came up. He only stood, and stared. He was staring at the man’s hands. Wren looked, and saw what he saw. They hung empty at his sides, brown and broad, working hands. And on the back of each there was a scar, round and deep and old, puckered at the edges, the shape a burn makes when something very hot has been held against the skin for a very long time. When he turned one hand a little, Wren saw the same scar on the palm. On both hands. As if, a long time ago, something had gone right through them. He was not a beggar this time, nor a ferryman, nor a voice in a chimney. It was the Lampwright himself, come up out of the Burned Country in the morning; and he had scars on his hands. Varrick looked at the scarred hands. Then, slowly, as if somebody else were moving his arm for him, he turned up his own right hand and looked at his palm, where the old pale mark of the Lamplighters’ oath-flame ran across it. He looked at it for a long time. The man said nothing to him. He only looked at Varrick, a few steps off, and his face was not angry. It was the look Old Ash used to have when he said lad, only more so — as if all the sorrow in Ash’s lad had been poured into one cup, and the cup were full to the brim and not spilling. Varrick’s sword fell out of his hand. It dropped into the ash with a soft thump and lay there. And then Captain Varrick turned and ran. He ran like a boy, clumsily, stumbling in the ash with his grey cloak tangling round his legs, and he did not look back. Down the slope he went and away across the plain, and the Hollow Knights went after him, drifting and stumbling, until the Queen’s camp was empty but for its tents, and its dead braziers, and a sword lying in the ash. Wren did not see them go. She was already running. There was nothing between her and Tobin now but a few yards of ash. She ran across it with the lamp blazing in her hands and dropped on her knees beside him. The colour had come back to everything on the hilltop, and not to him. He lay in the middle of it like a drawing in pencil on a painted page. “Tobin,” said Wren. “Tobin. Tobin.” She held the lamp out over him, close, as close as she dared. “Here. It’s for you. You don’t have to do anything. Please.” The lamp blazed. It blazed till her eyes watered. But it leaned away from Tobin, over her shoulder, towards somebody behind her; and Tobin did not move. Then the somebody behind her knelt down in the ash. He knelt on the other side of Tobin, and Wren did not look up at him. She could not. She saw a brown hand come down into the circle of the lamplight — a working hand, with a round old scar across the back of it — and lay itself, very gently, on Tobin’s grey head. It lay there, warm, the way a hand lies on the head of a child who is asleep and is not to be woken. “Tobin,” said the man. That was all he said. Only the name. He said it the way you say the name of somebody who has been lost a long time and has just this minute been found. Nothing happened. Then something did. It began at the top, in Tobin’s hair, under the man’s hand: a faint warmth coming up into the grey, like the first light of a fire in a cold room. It was gold — the untidy, ordinary, sticking-up-at-the-back gold of Tobin’s hair, coming back strand by strand under the scarred brown fingers, slowly, as if it were being poured. It came down over his forehead and into his eyebrows, which were fair and ridiculous and always looked surprised. It came into his face — the grey went out of his cheeks the way frost goes off a window when the sun gets to it — and pink came after. It came down his neck, and down his arms, all the way to his hands; and his hands, lying in the ash, were pink and ink-stained and ordinary, and in each palm was the round scar the size of the bottom of a little brass lamp. The frost went off his spectacles. Tobin breathed in — a long breath that caught in the middle, the way a breath catches when you have been under water a long time. He opened his eyes. He looked up — not at Wren; past her — at the man kneeling over him with one hand on his head. He looked for a long moment, blinking, the way you look at something very bright. His lips moved, and no sound came out of them. Wren found that she was crying. She had not noticed starting. Tears were running down her face and dripping off her chin onto Tobin’s shirt, and she did not care who saw, and she did not wipe them away. Cinder came trotting back up the slope, her tail blazing like a torch, and sat down beside the man as if she had always sat there, and looked from one of them to the other with her tongue out. The man looked at her. “Yes,” he said. “Well done. You’ve been very good. You can stop sitting on people now.” Cinder sneezed, a great shower of gold sparks, all over his sleeve. He brushed them off and did not seem to mind. “Mostly,” he said. Then he took his hand from Tobin’s head, and sat back on his heels, and looked across Tobin at Wren. He had kind eyes. That was the first thing she noticed, and afterwards it was the thing she remembered best. Not the colour of them. Only that they were kind, deep-set, with lines at the corners from laughing; and that they looked at her — at her cropped hair and her ash-black face and her red, wet, furious eyes — as if she were somebody worth looking at. Something tugged at her memory, hard, the way a fish tugs on a line. A smell of bread. A canal wall. A crate. “Wren,” he said. Nobody had said her name like that since a tower on a wall, and a pot of dreadful tea. She opened her mouth. Nothing came out of it. The man smiled. It began in his eyes and ended up somewhere in his beard; and he looked from her to Tobin, who was trying to sit up and could not quite manage it, and back again. “You two look half starved,” he said. “Hungry?”

fields.title: Breakfast by the Fire
fields.body_html:
The first piece of toast was black.

It was not a little brown at the edges. It was black all the way through, as black as the inside of a chimney, and when the man lifted it off the toasting-fork it was still smoking gently, like a small wet bonfire. He turned it over and looked at the other side, which was blacker.

Then he laughed.

He laughed out loud, sitting on his heels by the fire — a real laugh, a helpless one, the kind that comes up from under the ribs and will not be stopped — and Wren, on a stone across the fire with her arms round her knees, heard a sound come out of her own mouth that she did not recognise.

It was a laugh. A small cracked one, like a door that has not been opened all winter. She clapped her hand over her mouth, but it was too late. It was out.

“Well,” said the man, “that one’s yours, Cinder.”

Cinder took it from his fingers with great delicacy, carried it three steps away, and ate it, crunching loudly and looking at nobody, as if burnt toast were exactly what she had wanted all along.

They had come up to the top of the Hill together, slowly, in the cold bright morning.

Tobin could hardly walk. He leaned on Ash’s pole, and on the man’s arm; and Wren walked a little behind with the lamp, not helping and not going away, and not taking her eyes off him once.

At the top, by the workshop wall, was the little ring of stones where the Remnant had made their fire. The ashes were long cold. The man knelt down by them and raked them together with his fingers, and blew on them, once, quite gently, the way you blow on a spark you want to keep.

They caught.

I am not able to tell you where the basket came from. Wren never found out, and I do not think she ever asked. It was simply there by the fire when she next looked: a wide, flat basket with a cloth over it, and from under the cloth came a smell of new bread and a little drift of steam. Beside it was a heap of apples, so red in the morning light that Wren stared at them as if she had never seen an apple before, which in a way she had not.

The man went into the workshop and came out with a long iron toasting-fork from the wall. He had not looked for it. He had gone straight to it.

Now the second piece of toast was golden, and the apples were roasting in the edge of the fire, splitting their skins and hissing; and he held the toast out across the fire to Wren.

She looked at it. She looked at the hand holding it.

“How much?” she said.

It came out by itself, from Soot Lane and Mott’s yard. It was the oldest thing she knew how to say.

“No charge,” said the man.

“Everything’s got a charge.”

“Not this,” he said. “It’s given.”

Wren did not take the toast. She was looking at his face. At the lines at the corners of his eyes. At the eyes themselves, deep-set and kind, looking at her — at her tufty cropped hair and her sharp chin and her ash-black hands — as if she were somebody worth looking at. She had been hungry, once, outside a pawnshop in Crookback Market, and somebody with kind eyes had put a warm loaf into her hands and said those very words; and she had gone three steps, and thought of something cheeky to say, and turned round.

And he had not been there.

He was here.

Wren took the toast. She did not eat it, and she did not say anything at all, because her throat had closed up altogether. The man did not seem to need her to.

It was Cinder who heard them coming.

She sat up with her ears pricked and her mouth full of crust, and stared down the far slope of the Hill; and a moment later Wren heard it too — feet in the ash, and voices, and somebody laughing and crying at the same time, very loudly.

Then over the brow of the Hill came Mira, running.

She had the Chronicle clutched to her chest in both arms, which is not a good way to run uphill; and behind her, more slowly, came the Remnant, grimy and scratched, staring at the colour coming up out of the ground as if they were walking into a dream. In the middle of them, on her crutch, with her left arm strapped up in a sling made of somebody’s shawl, came Sister Hale. She was laughing and crying so hard that two people had to hold her up.

Mira did not stop running until she got to Wren. Then she dropped the Chronicle in the ash, which she would never have done in her right mind, and threw both arms round her.

“I heard it,” she said into Wren’s neck. “At dawn it sounded like the whole Hill breathing out. And then the colour came down the slope towards us like water, and we ran—“ She pulled back and held Wren at arm’s length and stared at her. “Your ribbon,” she said. “Wren, your ribbon. I didn’t know red could go as far as that.”

“Nor did I,” said Wren. Her voice was thick.

“And Tobin—“ Mira had seen him, sitting by the fire with Ash’s pole across his knees and his toast in his hand, pink and ink-stained and blinking. Her face crumpled up again. “Oh, Tobin. Oh, you idiot. We thought—“

“I know,” said Tobin. “I’m sorry. I’m — I’m all right, I think. Mostly.”

“There’s room by the fire,” said the man, behind them. “Come and sit down, all of you. There’s plenty. There is always room.”

Mira went quite still.

She did not turn round. She shut her eyes and tipped her head a little on one side, and Wren knew that she was not hearing the words at all. She was hearing the voice underneath them: low and warm and a little rough, like mist lying on a slow river.

Mira opened her eyes, and turned round, and looked at him.

He was sitting by the fire, turning an apple with the end of the toasting-fork. His hands were busy. She looked at them for a long moment — at the round old scar across the back of the one nearest her — and Wren saw her lips move, very slightly, as if she were counting.

“Your oar,” said Mira, in a small voice. “It creaks on the left.”

The man looked up at her and smiled.

“It always has,” he said.

Mira sat down in the ash where she was, quite suddenly, as though her knees had given way, and looked at him; and her face was so full of light that Wren had to look away.

Sister Hale had got to the fire by now. She stood leaning on her crutch, her old face working, and said, quite helplessly:

“Oh, duck—“

And stopped, with her good hand over her mouth, appalled.

The man laughed. It was the same laugh as at the toast: the real one, from under the ribs.

“Duck will do very well,” he said. “Sit down, Sister, before you fall down. Here. Mind the arm. You’ve been very brave, and you’ve been hurt, and you’ve not had any breakfast. Have an apple.”

Sister Hale sat down. She took the apple. She held it in her good hand and looked at it, and then at him, and two great tears ran down into the wrinkles of her face, one from the bright eye and one from the milky one.

“We only ever had the songs, Master,” she said. “All my life. Only ever the songs.”

“I know,” said the man. “I heard them. You sang them very well.” He paused. “Rather loud, some of them.”

And Sister Hale threw her head back and laughed her great cracked laugh, and the whole Remnant laughed with her, with their mouths full of toast; and the sound went up off the top of Cinder Hill, where, so far as anybody knew, nobody had laughed for three hundred years.

Tobin had not eaten his toast.

He sat a little apart from the others, at the edge of the firelight, with Ash’s pole across his knees and the toast going cold in his hand. He had not said anything since Mira. He was looking at his hands.

After a while the Lampwright came and sat down beside him.

He only sat there at first, with his elbows on his knees, looking out over the Burned Country; and Tobin, who had been waiting for something — a reckoning, a list — found that his heart had begun to thump.

Then the man reached across and laid his hand for a moment over Tobin’s — very lightly, so that it did not hurt.

It was warm, as it had been warm on the end of a cold dock, with the gulls going over and the tide gone out. And on the back of it was an old scar, pale and puckered, running right across it from side to side.

Tobin looked at the scar, and his breath caught, exactly as it had caught then. He did not say anything. He did not need to. He knew.

“Eat your toast,” said the man.

Tobin ate his toast, very slowly, because his hands were shaking; and when he had finished, the man said:

“Tobin, do you love me?”

Tobin looked up. He had thought there would be a great deal more to it than that. He found that the answer was there already, and had been for a long time, and was not at all difficult to say.

“Yes,” he said.

“Then keep my lamps,” said the man.

Tobin’s hand closed on Ash’s pole across his knees. He did not say anything. He only nodded.

They sat for a while. Over by the fire Mira was showing Sister Hale the colour of an apple — red, she was saying, but a different red from the ribbon, Sister; how many reds are there? — and the cobbler was trying to get a burnt crust back from Cinder, and failing.

“Tobin, do you love me?” said the man.

“Yes,” said Tobin. More quietly.

“Then look after the small ones.”

Tobin nodded again. He was looking at the ground now. Something was happening in his chest that he did not understand, a kind of tightening, the way a rope tightens when somebody begins to take up the slack.

And the man said, the third time, gently, “Tobin, do you love me?”

It hurt.

It was not a cruel question, or asked in a cruel way. But the third time it went straight in, under all the places he had been keeping safe, and found the sore place, and pressed on it; and Tobin, who had not cried on the end of the fish-dock, or on the road, or in the Queen’s camp with the grey coming up through his hands, put his face down and cried as if he would never stop.

“You know everything,” he said. It came out in pieces. “You know everything. You know I do.”

“Then follow me,” said the man.

He took Tobin’s hands. He took both of them, and turned them over, palm up, in his own; and Tobin, looking down through the tears and the one cracked lens, saw the two round scars on his own palms, the shape of the bottom of a little brass lamp. And round them, holding them, he saw the scars on the man’s palms.

They were the same shape.

The very same: round, and deep, and puckered at the edge, the shape a burn makes when you hold something very hot for a long time and do not let go. Only bigger, and older, and deeper, so that his own, lying inside them, looked like a child’s drawing of the real thing.

Tobin stared at them.

“They’re the same,” he said. His voice had gone odd. “Exactly the same shape. Only yours are — I’d say about half as big again — no, more, the diameter’s nearer twice—“ He stopped. He looked up. “Sorry. I’m — sorry. I don’t know why I’m measuring them.”

The man laughed. He did not let go of Tobin’s hands.

“I’d be worried if you didn’t,” he said.

Wren waited until the Lampwright had gone back to the fire. Then she got up and went and stood in front of Tobin, and Tobin looked up at her. His eyes were red. Hers were too, probably. She did not care.

She had thought all night of ways round it: a joke, or just giving him back the scarf and walking off, so that nobody would have to say anything.

If you have ever had to say sorry for something truly bad — not sorry I trod on your foot, but the other kind — you will know that it is one of the hardest things there is. It is harder than a fight. In a fight you can be angry, and anger is warm, and it holds you up. Saying sorry is like taking your coat off in the snow.

Wren had never taken her coat off for anybody in her life.

“I said I wished it had been you,” she said.

Her voice came out flat and hard, like a stone. Tobin did not say anything.

“In Vaelport. On the harbour wall. I said you sold him. I said I wished it had been you instead of him.” She swallowed. “And I’ve thought it was true ever since. I’ve walked all this way thinking it. Only then last night they were — you were going grey, and I was — and I didn’t. I don’t.” She stopped. Her face was burning. This was the worst part, and she knew it was coming, and she could not get round it. “It was the worst thing I ever said to anybody. And I’ve said some things. I’m sorry. I’m sorry, Tobin. Will you—“

She could not get the last bit out. It stuck.

She stood there with her fists clenched and her chin up and her eyes stinging, and it was a very long moment, and Cinder came and sat down exactly between their feet, the way she had sat by the fire on the night they all came, and looked up at both of them.

“Will you forgive me,” said Wren. “For it.”

“Yes,” said Tobin.

He did not make her wait for it. That was what she remembered afterwards. Not for one heartbeat, the way she would have made him wait. He said it at once, as if it had been ready in his mouth for days.

“Yes,” he said again. “Of course. Wren, I — it was true. I did sell him. I’m the one who—“

“Shut up,” said Wren. “I’m not finished.”

She took off the scarf. She unwound it from round her neck — twice round, the way it had been all the way from Vaelport — and held it out to him, all of it, in both hands.

“Here,” she said. “It’s yours. I never gave it back.”

Tobin looked at the scarf. He looked at her. Then he got up, slowly, leaning on Ash’s pole, and took it from her; and instead of putting it on, he put it round her neck again, twice round, carefully, the way you would wrap up somebody smaller than you who was going out in the cold. He tucked the end in.

Wren let him.

“It’s striped,” she said, after a moment. Her voice had gone wobbly. “Did you know it was striped?”

“Of course it’s striped,” said Tobin. “Green and blue. What did you think it was?”

“Grey,” said Wren. And then, because she was Wren, and could not help it: “If you tell anybody I said sorry, I’ll push you off this hill.”

Tobin considered the slope.

“Technically,” he said, “it’s a fairly gentle gradient on this side. You’d have to push quite hard.”

Wren hit him on the arm. Not very hard. And then — she was never sure afterwards which of them started it — she put her face against his shirt, and he put his arms round her, and they stood there on the top of Cinder Hill holding on to each other like two people on a roof in a high wind, while Cinder sat between their feet and looked pleased with herself, and nobody round the fire said a single word about it.

Later, when the Remnant were lying about in the warm ash like cats, Wren went and sat by the fire. The Lampwright was turning the last of the apples with the end of the toasting-fork, slowly, so that they did not burn. Wren watched his hands.

“Old Ash,” she said at last.

The man did not look up.

“He’s under the rock,” said Wren. “In Vaelport. At the bottom of the mine. There’s a whole mountain on top of him, and nobody even — there’s nothing. Nobody even got to say anything.” She stared at the fire. “He held the door. He held it so we could get out, and then it all came down, and he’s just gone. Lost. And I never even—“

“Wren,” said the man.

She stopped.

He said, “Old Ash isn’t lost. He’s waiting.”

He did not explain it. He did not say waiting for what, or where, and Wren did not ask him. She sat there with the words in her lap, turning them over like a smooth stone picked up on a beach; and they were warm, the way the ground was warm, all the way through.

After a long time she said, “And my mum and dad?”

She had never asked anybody that. Not Ash. Not anybody. She did not know she was going to ask it until it was out.

The man turned an apple over. He looked at her then, across the fire, with those kind deep-set eyes, and she saw that he knew exactly what she was asking, all of it — everything she did not know, and had never known, and was frightened to know.

“Trust me with them.”

Nothing more. And Wren, who had never trusted anybody with anything in her life, found that she could.

He went back to the apples.

And as he turned them, very softly, under his breath, the way a man hums who is busy with his hands and has forgotten anybody is listening, he began to hum a tune.

Wren knew it before the third note. She would have known it anywhere. She had known it all her life. Morning comes, morning comes — the old Lamplighter song, sung on the walls at the turning of the night, sung by more than one mother. Her mother’s song.

He hummed it slowly. He hummed it past the place where it always stopped for her, past and the dark shall not keep us, on into the part she did not have, the part nobody had ever been able to give her. She had heard it go that far once before, in a dream, by a cold forge, and woken too soon. It was only a hum. There were no words in it. But the tune went on, and climbed, and turned, and she sat absolutely still and held her breath and listened to it as she had never listened to anything —

And then he took an apple off the fire, and blew on it, and the tune stopped. Not at an ending. In the middle, the way a tune stops when somebody has simply put it down for a while and means to pick it up again later.

Wren did not ask him to finish it.

She never quite knew why — except that it seemed to her that it was not a song to be handed across a campfire like an apple. Not yet.

He held out the apple to her.

“Careful,” he said. “It’s hot.”

She took it.

Then he stood up, and stretched, and brushed the ash off his knees, and looked over his shoulder at the long low ruined building at the top of the Hill, where the doorway stood open and the tools hung waiting on the walls.

“Now,” he said. “Let’s go and see what you lot have been doing to my workshop.”

It was black all the way through, as black as the inside of a chimney, and when the man lifted it off the toasting-fork it was still smoking gently, like a small wet bonfire. He turned it over and looked at the other side, which was blacker. Then he laughed. He laughed out loud, sitting on his heels by the fire — a real laugh, a helpless one, the kind that comes up from under the ribs and will not be stopped — and Wren, on a stone across the fire with her arms round her knees, heard a sound come out of her own mouth that she did not recognise. It was a laugh. A small cracked one, like a door that has not been opened all winter. She clapped her hand over her mouth, but it was too late. It was out. “Well,” said the man, “that one’s yours, Cinder.” Cinder took it from his fingers with great delicacy, carried it three steps away, and ate it, crunching loudly and looking at nobody, as if burnt toast were exactly what she had wanted all along. They had come up to the top of the Hill together, slowly, in the cold bright morning. Tobin could hardly walk. He leaned on Ash’s pole, and on the man’s arm; and Wren walked a little behind with the lamp, not helping and not going away, and not taking her eyes off him once. At the top, by the workshop wall, was the little ring of stones where the Remnant had made their fire. The ashes were long cold. The man knelt down by them and raked them together with his fingers, and blew on them, once, quite gently, the way you blow on a spark you want to keep. They caught. I am not able to tell you where the basket came from. Wren never found out, and I do not think she ever asked. It was simply there by the fire when she next looked: a wide, flat basket with a cloth over it, and from under the cloth came a smell of new bread and a little drift of steam. Beside it was a heap of apples, so red in the morning light that Wren stared at them as if she had never seen an apple before, which in a way she had not. The man went into the workshop and came out with a long iron toasting-fork from the wall. He had not looked for it. He had gone straight to it. Now the second piece of toast was golden, and the apples were roasting in the edge of the fire, splitting their skins and hissing; and he held the toast out across the fire to Wren. She looked at it. She looked at the hand holding it. “How much?” she said. It came out by itself, from Soot Lane and Mott’s yard. It was the oldest thing she knew how to say. “No charge,” said the man. “Everything’s got a charge.” “Not this,” he said. “It’s given.” Wren did not take the toast. She was looking at his face. At the lines at the corners of his eyes. At the eyes themselves, deep-set and kind, looking at her — at her tufty cropped hair and her sharp chin and her ash-black hands — as if she were somebody worth looking at. She had been hungry, once, outside a pawnshop in Crookback Market, and somebody with kind eyes had put a warm loaf into her hands and said those very words; and she had gone three steps, and thought of something cheeky to say, and turned round. And he had not been there. He was here. Wren took the toast. She did not eat it, and she did not say anything at all, because her throat had closed up altogether. The man did not seem to need her to. It was Cinder who heard them coming. She sat up with her ears pricked and her mouth full of crust, and stared down the far slope of the Hill; and a moment later Wren heard it too — feet in the ash, and voices, and somebody laughing and crying at the same time, very loudly. Then over the brow of the Hill came Mira, running. She had the Chronicle clutched to her chest in both arms, which is not a good way to run uphill; and behind her, more slowly, came the Remnant, grimy and scratched, staring at the colour coming up out of the ground as if they were walking into a dream. In the middle of them, on her crutch, with her left arm strapped up in a sling made of somebody’s shawl, came Sister Hale. She was laughing and crying so hard that two people had to hold her up. Mira did not stop running until she got to Wren. Then she dropped the Chronicle in the ash, which she would never have done in her right mind, and threw both arms round her. “I heard it,” she said into Wren’s neck. “At dawn it sounded like the whole Hill breathing out. And then the colour came down the slope towards us like water, and we ran—“ She pulled back and held Wren at arm’s length and stared at her. “Your ribbon,” she said. “Wren, your ribbon. I didn’t know red could go as far as that.” “Nor did I,” said Wren. Her voice was thick. “And Tobin—“ Mira had seen him, sitting by the fire with Ash’s pole across his knees and his toast in his hand, pink and ink-stained and blinking. Her face crumpled up again. “Oh, Tobin. Oh, you idiot. We thought—“ “I know,” said Tobin. “I’m sorry. I’m — I’m all right, I think. Mostly.” “There’s room by the fire,” said the man, behind them. “Come and sit down, all of you. There’s plenty. There is always room.” Mira went quite still. She did not turn round. She shut her eyes and tipped her head a little on one side, and Wren knew that she was not hearing the words at all. She was hearing the voice underneath them: low and warm and a little rough, like mist lying on a slow river. Mira opened her eyes, and turned round, and looked at him. He was sitting by the fire, turning an apple with the end of the toasting-fork. His hands were busy. She looked at them for a long moment — at the round old scar across the back of the one nearest her — and Wren saw her lips move, very slightly, as if she were counting. “Your oar,” said Mira, in a small voice. “It creaks on the left.” The man looked up at her and smiled. “It always has,” he said. Mira sat down in the ash where she was, quite suddenly, as though her knees had given way, and looked at him; and her face was so full of light that Wren had to look away. Sister Hale had got to the fire by now. She stood leaning on her crutch, her old face working, and said, quite helplessly: “Oh, duck—“ And stopped, with her good hand over her mouth, appalled. The man laughed. It was the same laugh as at the toast: the real one, from under the ribs. “Duck will do very well,” he said. “Sit down, Sister, before you fall down. Here. Mind the arm. You’ve been very brave, and you’ve been hurt, and you’ve not had any breakfast. Have an apple.” Sister Hale sat down. She took the apple. She held it in her good hand and looked at it, and then at him, and two great tears ran down into the wrinkles of her face, one from the bright eye and one from the milky one. “We only ever had the songs, Master,” she said. “All my life. Only ever the songs.” “I know,” said the man. “I heard them. You sang them very well.” He paused. “Rather loud, some of them.” And Sister Hale threw her head back and laughed her great cracked laugh, and the whole Remnant laughed with her, with their mouths full of toast; and the sound went up off the top of Cinder Hill, where, so far as anybody knew, nobody had laughed for three hundred years. Tobin had not eaten his toast. He sat a little apart from the others, at the edge of the firelight, with Ash’s pole across his knees and the toast going cold in his hand. He had not said anything since Mira. He was looking at his hands. After a while the Lampwright came and sat down beside him. He only sat there at first, with his elbows on his knees, looking out over the Burned Country; and Tobin, who had been waiting for something — a reckoning, a list — found that his heart had begun to thump. Then the man reached across and laid his hand for a moment over Tobin’s — very lightly, so that it did not hurt. It was warm, as it had been warm on the end of a cold dock, with the gulls going over and the tide gone out. And on the back of it was an old scar, pale and puckered, running right across it from side to side. Tobin looked at the scar, and his breath caught, exactly as it had caught then. He did not say anything. He did not need to. He knew. “Eat your toast,” said the man. Tobin ate his toast, very slowly, because his hands were shaking; and when he had finished, the man said: “Tobin, do you love me?” Tobin looked up. He had thought there would be a great deal more to it than that. He found that the answer was there already, and had been for a long time, and was not at all difficult to say. “Yes,” he said. “Then keep my lamps,” said the man. Tobin’s hand closed on Ash’s pole across his knees. He did not say anything. He only nodded. They sat for a while. Over by the fire Mira was showing Sister Hale the colour of an apple — red, she was saying, but a different red from the ribbon, Sister; how many reds are there? — and the cobbler was trying to get a burnt crust back from Cinder, and failing. “Tobin, do you love me?” said the man. “Yes,” said Tobin. More quietly. “Then look after the small ones.” Tobin nodded again. He was looking at the ground now. Something was happening in his chest that he did not understand, a kind of tightening, the way a rope tightens when somebody begins to take up the slack. And the man said, the third time, gently, “Tobin, do you love me?” It hurt. It was not a cruel question, or asked in a cruel way. But the third time it went straight in, under all the places he had been keeping safe, and found the sore place, and pressed on it; and Tobin, who had not cried on the end of the fish-dock, or on the road, or in the Queen’s camp with the grey coming up through his hands, put his face down and cried as if he would never stop. “You know everything,” he said. It came out in pieces. “You know everything. You know I do.” “Then follow me,” said the man. He took Tobin’s hands. He took both of them, and turned them over, palm up, in his own; and Tobin, looking down through the tears and the one cracked lens, saw the two round scars on his own palms, the shape of the bottom of a little brass lamp. And round them, holding them, he saw the scars on the man’s palms. They were the same shape. The very same: round, and deep, and puckered at the edge, the shape a burn makes when you hold something very hot for a long time and do not let go. Only bigger, and older, and deeper, so that his own, lying inside them, looked like a child’s drawing of the real thing. Tobin stared at them. “They’re the same,” he said. His voice had gone odd. “Exactly the same shape. Only yours are — I’d say about half as big again — no, more, the diameter’s nearer twice—“ He stopped. He looked up. “Sorry. I’m — sorry. I don’t know why I’m measuring them.” The man laughed. He did not let go of Tobin’s hands. “I’d be worried if you didn’t,” he said. Wren waited until the Lampwright had gone back to the fire. Then she got up and went and stood in front of Tobin, and Tobin looked up at her. His eyes were red. Hers were too, probably. She did not care. She had thought all night of ways round it: a joke, or just giving him back the scarf and walking off, so that nobody would have to say anything. If you have ever had to say sorry for something truly bad — not sorry I trod on your foot, but the other kind — you will know that it is one of the hardest things there is. It is harder than a fight. In a fight you can be angry, and anger is warm, and it holds you up. Saying sorry is like taking your coat off in the snow. Wren had never taken her coat off for anybody in her life. “I said I wished it had been you,” she said. Her voice came out flat and hard, like a stone. Tobin did not say anything. “In Vaelport. On the harbour wall. I said you sold him. I said I wished it had been you instead of him.” She swallowed. “And I’ve thought it was true ever since. I’ve walked all this way thinking it. Only then last night they were — you were going grey, and I was — and I didn’t. I don’t.” She stopped. Her face was burning. This was the worst part, and she knew it was coming, and she could not get round it. “It was the worst thing I ever said to anybody. And I’ve said some things. I’m sorry. I’m sorry, Tobin. Will you—“ She could not get the last bit out. It stuck. She stood there with her fists clenched and her chin up and her eyes stinging, and it was a very long moment, and Cinder came and sat down exactly between their feet, the way she had sat by the fire on the night they all came, and looked up at both of them. “Will you forgive me,” said Wren. “For it.” “Yes,” said Tobin. He did not make her wait for it. That was what she remembered afterwards. Not for one heartbeat, the way she would have made him wait. He said it at once, as if it had been ready in his mouth for days. “Yes,” he said again. “Of course. Wren, I — it was true. I did sell him. I’m the one who—“ “Shut up,” said Wren. “I’m not finished.” She took off the scarf. She unwound it from round her neck — twice round, the way it had been all the way from Vaelport — and held it out to him, all of it, in both hands. “Here,” she said. “It’s yours. I never gave it back.” Tobin looked at the scarf. He looked at her. Then he got up, slowly, leaning on Ash’s pole, and took it from her; and instead of putting it on, he put it round her neck again, twice round, carefully, the way you would wrap up somebody smaller than you who was going out in the cold. He tucked the end in. Wren let him. “It’s striped,” she said, after a moment. Her voice had gone wobbly. “Did you know it was striped?” “Of course it’s striped,” said Tobin. “Green and blue. What did you think it was?” “Grey,” said Wren. And then, because she was Wren, and could not help it: “If you tell anybody I said sorry, I’ll push you off this hill.” Tobin considered the slope. “Technically,” he said, “it’s a fairly gentle gradient on this side. You’d have to push quite hard.” Wren hit him on the arm. Not very hard. And then — she was never sure afterwards which of them started it — she put her face against his shirt, and he put his arms round her, and they stood there on the top of Cinder Hill holding on to each other like two people on a roof in a high wind, while Cinder sat between their feet and looked pleased with herself, and nobody round the fire said a single word about it. Later, when the Remnant were lying about in the warm ash like cats, Wren went and sat by the fire. The Lampwright was turning the last of the apples with the end of the toasting-fork, slowly, so that they did not burn. Wren watched his hands. “Old Ash,” she said at last. The man did not look up. “He’s under the rock,” said Wren. “In Vaelport. At the bottom of the mine. There’s a whole mountain on top of him, and nobody even — there’s nothing. Nobody even got to say anything.” She stared at the fire. “He held the door. He held it so we could get out, and then it all came down, and he’s just gone. Lost. And I never even—“ “Wren,” said the man. She stopped. He said, “Old Ash isn’t lost. He’s waiting.” He did not explain it. He did not say waiting for what, or where, and Wren did not ask him. She sat there with the words in her lap, turning them over like a smooth stone picked up on a beach; and they were warm, the way the ground was warm, all the way through. After a long time she said, “And my mum and dad?” She had never asked anybody that. Not Ash. Not anybody. She did not know she was going to ask it until it was out. The man turned an apple over. He looked at her then, across the fire, with those kind deep-set eyes, and she saw that he knew exactly what she was asking, all of it — everything she did not know, and had never known, and was frightened to know. “Trust me with them.” Nothing more. And Wren, who had never trusted anybody with anything in her life, found that she could. He went back to the apples. And as he turned them, very softly, under his breath, the way a man hums who is busy with his hands and has forgotten anybody is listening, he began to hum a tune. Wren knew it before the third note. She would have known it anywhere. She had known it all her life. Morning comes, morning comes — the old Lamplighter song, sung on the walls at the turning of the night, sung by more than one mother. Her mother’s song. He hummed it slowly. He hummed it past the place where it always stopped for her, past and the dark shall not keep us, on into the part she did not have, the part nobody had ever been able to give her. She had heard it go that far once before, in a dream, by a cold forge, and woken too soon. It was only a hum. There were no words in it. But the tune went on, and climbed, and turned, and she sat absolutely still and held her breath and listened to it as she had never listened to anything — And then he took an apple off the fire, and blew on it, and the tune stopped. Not at an ending. In the middle, the way a tune stops when somebody has simply put it down for a while and means to pick it up again later. Wren did not ask him to finish it. She never quite knew why — except that it seemed to her that it was not a song to be handed across a campfire like an apple. Not yet. He held out the apple to her. “Careful,” he said. “It’s hot.” She took it. Then he stood up, and stretched, and brushed the ash off his knees, and looked over his shoulder at the long low ruined building at the top of the Hill, where the doorway stood open and the tools hung waiting on the walls. “Now,” he said. “Let’s go and see what you lot have been doing to my workshop.”

fields.title: Carry My Flame
fields.body_html:
He went into the workshop the way a man goes into his own kitchen after a long time away: not slowly, not solemnly, but looking about him, noticing things.

The Remnant crowded in the doorway behind him and did not dare come further. Wren and Mira and Tobin came in, because nobody stopped them; and Cinder came in first of all, because nobody ever stopped Cinder.

It was the same long low room that Wren had found alone, days ago, with the dark coming down. The cold forges. The workbench. The tools hung neatly along the walls, each on its own peg, as if somebody had tidied up one evening meaning to start again in the morning. But it did not feel the same. It had felt, that first night, like a room holding its breath. Now it felt like a room that had let it out.

He hung the toasting-fork back on its peg, between the tongs and the little hammer. It fitted exactly.

Then he walked along the wall, slowly, and touched the tools as he passed them — not taking any down, only touching them, a fingertip on a handle here, a palm flat on the head of a mallet there, the way you might touch the heads of children in a row. He stopped at the bench and looked at the half-finished lamp lying on it, with its brass body and its empty top where the chimney should have gone. He picked it up and turned it over in his scarred hands, and set it down again, very gently, exactly where it had been.

And then he turned round and looked at the racks.

A hundred small brass lamps, row on row, every one of them finished except for the last part: no chimney, no wick, no flame. They stood on their shelves in the grey light from the doorway like a choir that has been waiting a very long time for somebody to give it the note.

The Lampwright looked at them.

He did not say anything. He stood in the middle of his workshop with his hands at his sides and looked at the hundred unfinished lamps for a long, long time; and then, slowly, he smiled. It was not the laugh from the toast. It was quieter than that, and it went deeper, and it was the kind of smile a person smiles when he is looking at something he has been looking forward to for years and years, and it is nearly here.

Tobin opened his mouth.

Mira put her hand on his arm, very lightly, and he shut it again.

I have often wondered what he was thinking, standing there among his lamps. I believe I know, now. But this is not the place to tell it; the children only knew that whatever it was, it made him glad.

The iron door at the back of the workshop stood open, the way Tobin had left it the night he fitted his mother’s compass into the lock. Mira went to the Lampwright with the Chronicle in her arms. She had wiped the ash off its cover with her sleeve.

“This is yours, I think,” she said.

He took it from her. He did not open it at the beginning. He opened it near the end, as if he knew exactly where to look, and found the last written page, and read the last written line. Wren could not see it from where she stood. She did not need to. She knew it by heart, and so did all of them. On the third morning, the fire woke.

He read it. He smiled at it, the same smile as at the lamps. Then he closed the book and put it back into Mira’s arms.

“Look after it,” he said.

Mira held it tight against her chest and nodded, and could not say anything.

Wren had been standing by the cold forge with the lamp in her hands, working up to something, the way she had worked up to Tobin. It was no easier the second time.

She went to him and held it out.

“Here,” she said. “It’s yours. It always was. It’s your own lamp — Ash said so, the one you carried down the Mountain. You should have it back. You can do far more with it than I can. I nearly—“ Her voice wobbled. “I nearly let it go out. In the tent. I had it right up to my mouth.”

“I know,” said the Lampwright.

“So you should have it.”

He did not take it. He put out his hands and folded them round hers — round her hands, and the lamp inside them, both together — so that she could feel the scars, warm and rough, against her knuckles.

“It was given, Wren. Not lost.”

Wren stood very still.

She was in her garret in Soot Lane, on a night a very long time ago, with the grate cold and the lamp sitting on her windowsill where it had come back to her yet again, and she was telling it off for following her about. And a voice had come down the chimney. Low and kind. It was given, child. Not lost. She had been frightened then, for the first time she could remember, and comforted at the same time, and she had never told anyone, not even Ash.

She looked up at him.

He let go of her hands. The lamp stayed in them, burning gold, leaning a little towards him the way it always would now, and warm against her fingers as it had been the very first night, when she had stuffed it inside her coat in a sealed-up flue and run.

“Keep it,” he said. “You’ll want it. You’ve a long way to carry it yet.”

They stayed on the Hill that day, and that night.

It was a quiet sort of day, and quiet days are hard to tell. The Lampwright mended Sister Hale’s crutch, which had cracked in the scramble down the Hill, with a strip of brass from his own bench, and told her it would now outlast her, and she told him that was not saying much. He walked round the top of the Hill with the smallest of the Remnant’s children holding on to two of his fingers, and showed her where the green things were coming up out of the ash, and let her give them names. Cinder followed him everywhere. If he sat down, she sat on his feet. If he stood up, she stood up. Once he stepped over her, and she was so offended that she sneezed a shower of gold sparks onto his boots, and he apologised to her very gravely, and she forgave him at once.

And the colour went on coming back. All day it spread down the sides of the Hill from the top, slowly, the way warmth spreads through a cold room from a fire: brown and black and rust and green, and the red of the rock showing through. By evening it had reached the empty grey tents of the Queen’s camp below, and gone round them, and on.

Night came.

It came the way nights always came in Gloamhaven, quickly and very dark; and the Remnant settled in heaps round the fire, and Sister Hale sang them something old and quiet in her cracked strong voice, and one by one they went to sleep.

Tobin woke in the middle of it.

He did not know what had woken him. He lay in the warm ash with his head on his arm and looked up at the dark — the real, thick, black dark of the Burned Country at midnight, with no moon and no Ring-lamp for a hundred miles — and waited for his hands to start shaking.

They did not shake.

He thought of his mother’s little night-lamp, and found he could not remember the last time he had wanted it. He had been afraid of the dark every night of his life since he was five years old. And now here he was, lying in the very middle of it, on the hill where the dark had come up like a tide —

And it was only dark. That was all. It was only the night, and the night was warm.

He sat up. The fire had burned down to red, and somebody was sitting beside it, feeding it a stick at a time.

Tobin went and sat down next to him. Neither of them said anything for a while.

“May I ask you something?” said Tobin at last.

“You may.”

“It’s a question I asked Old Ash, in the Leaning Tower, the night he told us about you with shadows on a sheet.” Tobin took a breath. “If you lit a thousand lamps from one flame — and you did, in the story, every lamp in every city — then by the end there ought to be nothing left. That’s just arithmetic. Only there was. There always is. Wren gave it to the whole Beacon in Emberwick and it was no smaller after. And I’ve never been able to make it come out. Ash said to hold the question. To keep it in my pocket. He said it was a good one.”

The Lampwright put another stick on the fire, and watched it catch.

“And have you kept it?”

“Yes. All this time.”

“Then keep it a little longer,” said the Lampwright. “It’s nearly ripe.”

Tobin thought about this. He found, rather to his own surprise, that it was a perfectly good answer, and that he did not mind at all.

They sat by the fire together until Tobin’s head began to nod, and then he lay down again, beside it this time, in the warm, and went to sleep with the dark all round him; and he did not dream of anything at all.

The Lampwright woke them before the sun was up.

He did not shake anybody. He simply stood up by the fire, and somehow everybody on the Hill was awake at once and sitting up, rubbing their eyes, looking at him. The sky in the east was going grey. It was cold, the way mornings were always cold. But the ground under them was warm.

“Come and see,” he said.

He took them to the eastern brow of the Hill, where it sloped away down into the Burned Country. They stood in a ragged line in the half-light — Sister Hale on her mended crutch, the Remnant in their heaps of shawls, Mira with the Chronicle, Tobin with Ash’s pole, Wren with the lamp, and Cinder sitting on the Lampwright’s left boot — and looked out.

The whole of Gloamhaven lay round them, if you could have seen far enough. The plains of ash. The Scarecrow Farms, where grey people stood in grey fields and did not come in. The coast hills, and Vaelport on the far side of them, with its dead stones. Emberwick, and the Greywaste, and Deepholm under the ground. And other cities that none of them had ever seen, each with its Ring of lamps on its walls, burning dimmer every year; and between the cities, all the miles and miles of places that had no Ring at all.

“Carry my Flame,” said the Lampwright, “to every Ring. And past them.”

Nobody said anything for a moment.

“Past them?” said Mira.

“Past the walls,” said the Lampwright. “Into the farms, and the mines, and the boats, and the places nobody has bothered to put a lamp. Anywhere a door is shut. Anywhere anybody is sitting in the grey.” He looked along the line at them, one by one: at the Remnant, and Sister Hale, and Mira, and Tobin, and Wren. “Anyone who asks. Rich and poor. Kind and unkind. And never charge a penny.”

Wren thought of the Heskeths’ kitchen, and the thin soup, and Posy sitting up in bed asking for bread. She thought of the grey man in the field who had turned his head towards the house.

“With one lamp?” she said. It came out sharper than she meant. It always did. “There’s hundreds of people out there. Thousands. There’s one lamp. And there’s—“ she looked along the line — “not twenty of us. Counting the fox.”

The Lampwright looked at her, and his eyes were laughing.

“What is given—“ he said.

And Wren, who had first heard that in a tower on a wall and not believed a word of it, heard herself finish it.

“—grows,” she said.

“Well, then,” said the Lampwright.

He turned and looked out to the east, where the grey was getting paler.

“At Midsummer,” he said, “there will be a gift. For all of you. Wait for it.” He looked back at them, and at Wren last of all. “You won’t carry it alone.”

“What gift?” said Tobin at once. “What kind of — how will we know when—“

“You’ll know,” said the Lampwright, and Tobin, for the second time in two days, found that this was a perfectly good answer.

Then the Lampwright bent down and scratched Cinder between the ears, and said something to her that nobody else could hear, and she sat back on her haunches and looked up at him with her tail curled round her feet and her spark burning bright and steady. And he walked away from them, down the eastern slope of Cinder Hill, towards the morning.

Wren ran after him.

She had not meant to. Her feet did it before the rest of her had decided. She ran down the slope in the warm ash, with the lamp in her hand and the striped scarf flying, and she was thinking, the whole way, of a market and a crate and three steps; of a river and a mist and a boat that was not there; of all the times she had turned round to say something and found nobody to say it to.

“Wait,” she said. “Wait—“

He stopped. He turned round. He waited for her.

She stopped in front of him, out of breath, and found that she did not know what to say after all. She had never been any good at it. She had said rot and blast and you great lump all her life, and how much, and everything costs. She had hardly ever said the other thing. It was not a Soot Lane word.

She said it anyway.

“Thank you,” said Wren.

He smiled at her. It started in his eyes, and went down into the lines at the corners of them, and ended up in his beard.

“You’re welcome, Wren,” he said.

Then he turned and went on down the hill, and she stood and watched him. She watched him all the way down the slope, and out onto the edge of the plain, where the ash ran out to meet the sky; and the colour came up behind him in his footprints, brown and green, a thin bright path going east. Behind her the others had come to the brow. She heard them come. She heard Mira catch her breath, and Tobin say oh very quietly, and Sister Hale begin, under her breath, to sing.

The sun came up.

It came up right in front of him, over the far edge of the Burned Country, and for a moment he was a dark shape against it, walking — no bigger than one of Ash’s paper puppets on a sheet, a little figure of a man going on through the towns.

And then he was not there.

Wren blinked. She looked along the line of the plain, and up and down it, and back again. There was nothing on it. There was only the path of colour going out from the foot of the Hill, brown and green, as far as she could see — and then the plain, and the sun.

She did not feel the way she had felt at the canal wall in Crookback Market, with her mouth open and the crate empty. She did not feel the way she had felt on the bank of the Gloam River. She stood there in the warm ash, and she found that she was not frightened, and not cheated, and not even very sad. He was not gone the way Ash had seemed gone. He was gone the way somebody goes into the next room. You know he is there. You can hear him moving about.

Cinder came down the slope and sat beside her, and looked out after him.

She did not whine. She did not run after him. She sat very upright with her tail round her feet, the way she had sat on the harbour wall at Vaelport watching three roads, and the spark at the end of her tail was burning bright and gold and steady, like a lamp in a window that somebody has lit and means to keep lit, for as long as it takes.

They stood on the brow of Cinder Hill for a long time after that, all of them together.

Nobody said very much. There did not seem to be any need. They knew now, every one of them, what Old Ash had known that day on the bank of the Gloam River, when he leaned on his two poles and smiled and would not say why. And they knew, too, where he had been: in the market, and in the chimney, and in the boat, and on the dock — never more than a step or two out of sight.

Tobin was leaning on Ash’s pole. Mira was holding the Chronicle. Wren was holding the lamp. Sister Hale had stopped singing and was simply standing, with her good arm round as many of the Remnant as she could reach, and her one bright eye shining.

And the sun went on coming up.

It came up over the Burned Country, and over the black round Hill, and over the long low workshop with its hundred lamps waiting on their shelves; and I will not tell you it was golden, because it was not. Not yet. It was still the pale cursed sun of Gloamhaven, like a coin seen through dirty water, the same sun it had been for three hundred years.

Wren, who had never in her life liked beginnings, because in her experience they always cost you something later, tucked the lamp inside her coat against her ribs, and wound the striped scarf twice round her neck, and turned to the others, and grinned.

“Well,” she said. “Come on, then. It’s a long way to everywhere.”

Nobody moved, quite yet. Because Mira had lifted her face to the east, and then Tobin, and then Sister Hale and all the Remnant, one by one, and last of all Wren — as if they had all felt the same thing at the same moment, and could not quite believe it, and did not want to be the first to say so.

It was only a little. You might not have noticed it, if you had not been standing there. But it was there, and it was true, and it was a beginning.

For the first time in three hundred years, the sun over Cinder Hill looked a little warmer.
fields.body_text: He went into the workshop the way a man goes into his own kitchen after a long time away: not slowly, not solemnly, but looking about him, noticing things. The Remnant crowded in the doorway behind him and did not dare come further. Wren and Mira and Tobin came in, because nobody stopped them; and Cinder came in first of all, because nobody ever stopped Cinder. It was the same long low room that Wren had found alone, days ago, with the dark coming down. The cold forges. The workbench. The tools hung neatly along the walls, each on its own peg, as if somebody had tidied up one evening meaning to start again in the morning. But it did not feel the same. It had felt, that first night, like a room holding its breath. Now it felt like a room that had let it out. He hung the toasting-fork back on its peg, between the tongs and the little hammer. It fitted exactly. Then he walked along the wall, slowly, and touched the tools as he passed them — not taking any down, only touching them, a fingertip on a handle here, a palm flat on the head of a mallet there, the way you might touch the heads of children in a row. He stopped at the bench and looked at the half-finished lamp lying on it, with its brass body and its empty top where the chimney should have gone. He picked it up and turned it over in his scarred hands, and set it down again, very gently, exactly where it had been. And then he turned round and looked at the racks. A hundred small brass lamps, row on row, every one of them finished except for the last part: no chimney, no wick, no flame. They stood on their shelves in the grey light from the doorway like a choir that has been waiting a very long time for somebody to give it the note. The Lampwright looked at them. He did not say anything. He stood in the middle of his workshop with his hands at his sides and looked at the hundred unfinished lamps for a long, long time; and then, slowly, he smiled. It was not the laugh from the toast. It was quieter than that, and it went deeper, and it was the kind of smile a person smiles when he is looking at something he has been looking forward to for years and years, and it is nearly here. Tobin opened his mouth. Mira put her hand on his arm, very lightly, and he shut it again. I have often wondered what he was thinking, standing there among his lamps. I believe I know, now. But this is not the place to tell it; the children only knew that whatever it was, it made him glad. The iron door at the back of the workshop stood open, the way Tobin had left it the night he fitted his mother’s compass into the lock. Mira went to the Lampwright with the Chronicle in her arms. She had wiped the ash off its cover with her sleeve. “This is yours, I think,” she said. He took it from her. He did not open it at the beginning. He opened it near the end, as if he knew exactly where to look, and found the last written page, and read the last written line. Wren could not see it from where she stood. She did not need to. She knew it by heart, and so did all of them. On the third morning, the fire woke. He read it. He smiled at it, the same smile as at the lamps. Then he closed the book and put it back into Mira’s arms. “Look after it,” he said. Mira held it tight against her chest and nodded, and could not say anything. Wren had been standing by the cold forge with the lamp in her hands, working up to something, the way she had worked up to Tobin. It was no easier the second time. She went to him and held it out. “Here,” she said. “It’s yours. It always was. It’s your own lamp — Ash said so, the one you carried down the Mountain. You should have it back. You can do far more with it than I can. I nearly—“ Her voice wobbled. “I nearly let it go out. In the tent. I had it right up to my mouth.” “I know,” said the Lampwright. “So you should have it.” He did not take it. He put out his hands and folded them round hers — round her hands, and the lamp inside them, both together — so that she could feel the scars, warm and rough, against her knuckles. “It was given, Wren. Not lost.” Wren stood very still. She was in her garret in Soot Lane, on a night a very long time ago, with the grate cold and the lamp sitting on her windowsill where it had come back to her yet again, and she was telling it off for following her about. And a voice had come down the chimney. Low and kind. It was given, child. Not lost. She had been frightened then, for the first time she could remember, and comforted at the same time, and she had never told anyone, not even Ash. She looked up at him. He let go of her hands. The lamp stayed in them, burning gold, leaning a little towards him the way it always would now, and warm against her fingers as it had been the very first night, when she had stuffed it inside her coat in a sealed-up flue and run. “Keep it,” he said. “You’ll want it. You’ve a long way to carry it yet.” They stayed on the Hill that day, and that night. It was a quiet sort of day, and quiet days are hard to tell. The Lampwright mended Sister Hale’s crutch, which had cracked in the scramble down the Hill, with a strip of brass from his own bench, and told her it would now outlast her, and she told him that was not saying much. He walked round the top of the Hill with the smallest of the Remnant’s children holding on to two of his fingers, and showed her where the green things were coming up out of the ash, and let her give them names. Cinder followed him everywhere. If he sat down, she sat on his feet. If he stood up, she stood up. Once he stepped over her, and she was so offended that she sneezed a shower of gold sparks onto his boots, and he apologised to her very gravely, and she forgave him at once. And the colour went on coming back. All day it spread down the sides of the Hill from the top, slowly, the way warmth spreads through a cold room from a fire: brown and black and rust and green, and the red of the rock showing through. By evening it had reached the empty grey tents of the Queen’s camp below, and gone round them, and on. Night came. It came the way nights always came in Gloamhaven, quickly and very dark; and the Remnant settled in heaps round the fire, and Sister Hale sang them something old and quiet in her cracked strong voice, and one by one they went to sleep. Tobin woke in the middle of it. He did not know what had woken him. He had been afraid of the dark every night of his life since he was five years old. The fire had burned down to red, and somebody was sitting beside it, feeding it a stick at a time. Tobin went and sat down next to him. Neither of them said anything for a while. “May I ask you something?” said Tobin at last. “You may.” “It’s a question I asked Old Ash, in the Leaning Tower, the night he told us about you with shadows on a sheet.” Tobin took a breath. “If you lit a thousand lamps from one flame — and you did, in the story, every lamp in every city — then by the end there ought to be nothing left. That’s just arithmetic. Only there was. There always is. Wren gave it to the whole Beacon in Emberwick and it was no smaller after. And I’ve never been able to make it come out. Ash said to hold the question. To keep it in my pocket. He said it was a good one.” The Lampwright put another stick on the fire, and watched it catch. “And have you kept it?” “Yes. All this time.” “Then keep it a little longer,” said the Lampwright. “It’s nearly ripe.” Tobin thought about this. He found, rather to his own surprise, that it was a perfectly good answer, and that he did not mind at all. They sat by the fire together until Tobin’s head began to nod, and then he lay down again, beside it this time, in the warm, and went to sleep with the dark all round him; and he did not dream of anything at all. He simply stood up by the fire, and somehow everybody on the Hill was awake at once and sitting up, rubbing their eyes, looking at him. The sky in the east was going grey. It was cold, the way mornings were always cold. But the ground under them was warm. “Come and see,” he said. He took them to the eastern brow of the Hill, where it sloped away down into the Burned Country. They stood in a ragged line in the half-light — Sister Hale on her mended crutch, the Remnant in their heaps of shawls, Mira with the Chronicle, Tobin with Ash’s pole, Wren with the lamp, and Cinder sitting on the Lampwright’s left boot — and looked out. The whole of Gloamhaven lay round them, if you could have seen far enough. The plains of ash. The Scarecrow Farms, where grey people stood in grey fields and did not come in. The coast hills, and Vaelport on the far side of them, with its dead stones. Emberwick, and the Greywaste, and Deepholm under the ground. And other cities that none of them had ever seen, each with its Ring of lamps on its walls, burning dimmer every year; and between the cities, all the miles and miles of places that had no Ring at all. “Carry my Flame,” said the Lampwright, “to every Ring. And past them.” Nobody said anything for a moment. “Past them?” said Mira. “Past the walls,” said the Lampwright. “Into the farms, and the mines, and the boats, and the places nobody has bothered to put a lamp. Anywhere a door is shut. Anywhere anybody is sitting in the grey.” He looked along the line at them, one by one: at the Remnant, and Sister Hale, and Mira, and Tobin, and Wren. “Anyone who asks. Rich and poor. Kind and unkind. And never charge a penny.” Wren thought of the Heskeths’ kitchen, and the thin soup, and Posy sitting up in bed asking for bread. She thought of the grey man in the field who had turned his head towards the house. “With one lamp?” she said. It came out sharper than she meant. It always did. “There’s hundreds of people out there. Thousands. There’s one lamp. And there’s—“ she looked along the line — “not twenty of us. Counting the fox.” The Lampwright looked at her, and his eyes were laughing. “What is given—“ he said. And Wren, who had first heard that in a tower on a wall and not believed a word of it, heard herself finish it. “—grows,” she said. “Well, then,” said the Lampwright. He turned and looked out to the east, where the grey was getting paler. “At Midsummer,” he said, “there will be a gift. For all of you. Wait for it.” He looked back at them, and at Wren last of all. “You won’t carry it alone.” “What gift?” said Tobin at once. “What kind of — how will we know when—“ “You’ll know,” said the Lampwright, and Tobin, for the second time in two days, found that this was a perfectly good answer. Then the Lampwright bent down and scratched Cinder between the ears, and said something to her that nobody else could hear, and she sat back on her haunches and looked up at him with her tail curled round her feet and her spark burning bright and steady. He turned round. He waited for her. She stopped in front of him, out of breath, and found that she did not know what to say after all. She had never been any good at it.
